previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease, and a history of bilateral lower extremity amputations was admitted for hyperkalemia and worsening kidney function, with a creatinine of 12.3 and potassium of 6.6. She was treated acutely with insulin, calcium, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate. Admission was complicated by accidental arterial puncture during left internal jugular central line placement, resulting in a hematocrit drop from 27.3 to 22.3, requiring transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells and suturing. A tunneled dialysis catheter was placed on hospital day two, and hemodialysis was initiated, leading to improvement in renal parameters. She was found to have a urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, sensitive to ciprofloxacin, and was treated with a short course of antibiotics. The patient was discharged home with services to begin outpatient dialysis, with follow-up planned for fistula creation and continued management of chronic conditions including diabetes, systolic heart failure, and anemia.

Brief Hospital Course: #Shakiness and nausea: The cause for the patient's symptoms were thought to be multifactorial, likely secondary to a possible UTI, anxiety, and a possible medication effect. It is difficult to say whether or not she truly had a UTI as her UA results came from a Foley bag and she was afebrile with a normal WBC count. Because her symptoms improved so drastically only 30 minutes after antibiotics were administered, there is likely some anxiety component to her presentation. Finally, gabapentin is renally cleared and could cause some of her shakiness symptoms, and thus was also thought as a potential etiology. While the patient was in the hospital she remained afebrile and asymptomatic with a normal WBC count. She received her normally scheduled dialysis on the first day of admission. Her Foley was also changed that day and a repeat UA and Urine culture were sent (repeat UA showing similar results to UA on admission, repeat urine culture pending at time of discharge). By the second day of admission she was feeling completely at baseline. Final thought was that her symptoms were more consistent with chronic colonization of her urinary system (versus an active UTI) and thus antibiotics were not given during admission. Furthermore, there was concern that antibiotic use would breed a multidrug resistant organism. Gabapentin was also discontinued during her admission and resumed at a lower dose upon discharge. #Chronic: 1. CKD: During admission her electrolytes and creatinine were trended, showing improvement in values after dialysis. 2. DM1: Patient was continued on home glargine and a humalog sliding scale. 3. HTN: The patient was hypertensive on admission, but may not have taken her medications earlier in the day. With monitoring and administration of her home medications she returned to baseline. 4. CAD: Home ASA was given 5. Urinary spasm: Home oxybutynin was given 6. Phantom Pain: Home oxycodone, oxycontin, and lidocaine were given.
